Ex 7.1 Q1:
\(r = 1.5\) cm, \(h = 5\) cm.

Volume of a cone \(= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times (1.5)^2 \times 5\)

\(= \dfrac{22 \times 2.25 \times 5}{21} = \dfrac{247.5}{21}\)

\(= 11.79\ \text{cm}^3\) (approx.)

\(\therefore\) the volume of the cone is about \(11.79\ \text{cm}^3\).
Ex 7.1 Q2:
Diameter \(= 6\) cm, so \(r = 3\) cm.

Volume of a sphere \(= \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3\)

\(= \dfrac{4}{3} \times 3.14 \times 3^3\)

\(= \dfrac{4}{3} \times 3.14 \times 27 = 4 \times 3.14 \times 9\)

\(= 113.04\ \text{cm}^3\)

\(\therefore\) the volume of the sphere is \(113.04\ \text{cm}^3\).
Ex 7.1 Q3:
\(r = 5\) cm, \(h = 40\) cm, \(\pi = 3.14\).

Total surface area of a cylinder \(= 2\pi r\,(r + h)\)

\(= 2 \times 3.14 \times 5 \times (5 + 40)\)

\(= 2 \times 3.14 \times 5 \times 45\)

\(= 1413\ \text{sq.cm}\)

\(\therefore\) the total surface area of the cylinder is 1413 sq.cm.
Ex 7.1 Q4:
\(r = 7\) cm.

Surface area of a sphere \(= 4\pi r^2\)

\(= 4 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7^2\)

\(= 4 \times 22 \times 7\)

\(= 616\ \text{sq.cm}\)

\(\therefore\) the surface area of the sphere is 616 sq.cm.
Ex 7.1 Q5:
Volume of the cuboid \(= l \times b \times h = 44 \times 21 \times 12 = 11088\ \text{cm}^3\).

Melting does not change the volume, so the cone has the same volume.

Volume of the cone \(= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h\)

\(11088 = \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times r^2 \times 24\)

\(11088 = \dfrac{22 \times 8}{7} \times r^2 = \dfrac{176}{7}r^2\)

\(\therefore r^2 = \dfrac{11088 \times 7}{176} = 441\)

\(\therefore\) the radius of the base of the cone is 21 cm.
Ex 7.1 Q6:
Cylindrical pot: \(r = 7\) cm, \(h = 10\) cm.

Volume \(= \pi r^2 h = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 49 \times 10 = 1540\ \text{cm}^3\)

Conical jug: \(r = 3.5\) cm, \(h = 10\) cm.

Volume \(= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h = \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times (3.5)^2 \times 10 = \dfrac{2695}{21} = 128.33\ \text{cm}^3\)

Number of jugs \(= \dfrac{\text{volume of the pot}}{\text{volume of one jug}} = \dfrac{1540}{128.33} = 12\)

\(\therefore\) the cylindrical pot holds 12 jugs of water.
Ex 7.1 Q7:

Volume of the cylinder \(= \pi r^2 \times 3 = 100 \times 3 = 300\ \text{cm}^3\)

Volume of the whole figure \(= 500\ \text{cm}^3\)

Ex 7.4 Q1:
[Textbook note: the book's printed answer for this question is 3.92 sq.cm, which is what the segment would measure if the \(45^\circ\) were the angle at the CENTRE. Three things agree that the \(45^\circ\) belongs at B: the stem says \(\angle\) ABC, the angle arc in Fig. 7.43 is drawn at B, and the figure is to scale \(-\) chord BC subtends about \(95^\circ\) at the centre of the circle as drawn. Since A is the centre, AB and AC are radii and the central angle \(\angle\) BAC is \(90^\circ\), so the segment is 28 sq.cm. The correct answer is 28 sq.cm.]

A is the centre, so AB and AC are radii and AB \(=\) AC \(= 7\sqrt{2}\) cm.

\(\therefore \triangle\) ABC is isosceles, so \(\angle\) ACB \(= \angle\) ABC \(= 45^\circ\).

\(\therefore \angle\) BAC \(= 180^\circ - 45^\circ - 45^\circ = 90^\circ\), i.e. \(\theta = 90^\circ\) and \(r^2 = (7\sqrt{2})^2 = 98\).

A(sector A-BXC) \(= \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2 = \dfrac{90}{360} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 98\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{4} \times 308 = 77\ \text{sq.cm}\)

A(\(\triangle\) ABC) \(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{AB} \times \text{AC}\)  (the angle between them is \(90^\circ\))

\(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 7\sqrt{2} \times 7\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 98 = 49\ \text{sq.cm}\)

A(segment BXC) \(=\) A(sector A-BXC) \(-\) A(\(\triangle\) ABC)

\(= 77 - 49 = 28\ \text{sq.cm}\)

\(\therefore\) the area of segment BXC is 28 sq.cm. (With \(\pi = 3.14\) instead of \(\frac{22}{7}\) the same working gives 27.93 sq.cm.)

\(h = 21\) cm, \(r_1 = 20\) cm, \(r_2 = 15\) cm, \(\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}\).

Capacity \(=\) volume of the frustum \(= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi h\left(r_1^{\,2} + r_2^{\,2} + r_1 r_2\right)\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 21 \times (400 + 225 + 300)\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{3} \times 22 \times 3 \times 925\)

\(= 20.35\) litre

PS7 Q3:
Volume of one ball \(= \dfrac{4}{3}\pi (1)^3 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi\ \text{cm}^3\)

The tube is a hollow cylinder. Outer radius \(R = 30\) cm and the thickness is 2 cm, so the inner radius is \(r = 30 - 2 = 28\) cm; the length is \(h = 90\) cm.

Volume of the tube \(= \pi h\left(R^2 - r^2\right)\)

\(= \pi \times 90 \times (900 - 784)\)

\(= \pi \times 90 \times 116 = 10440\pi\ \text{cm}^3\)

Melting preserves volume, so

number of balls \(= \dfrac{10440\pi}{\frac{4}{3}\pi} = \dfrac{10440 \times 3}{4} = 7830\)

\(\therefore\) 7830 balls were melted to make the tube.
PS7 Q4:
Volume of the parallelopiped \(= 16 \times 11 \times 10 = 1760\ \text{cm}^3\)

Each coin is a cylinder of diameter 2 cm, so \(r = 1\) cm, and thickness \(2\ \text{mm} = 0.2\) cm.

Volume of one coin \(= \pi r^2 h = \pi \times 1 \times 0.2 = 0.2\pi\ \text{cm}^3\)

Number of coins \(= \dfrac{1760}{0.2\pi} = \dfrac{8800}{\pi} = \dfrac{8800 \times 7}{22}\)   \(\left(\text{taking } \pi = \dfrac{22}{7}\right)\)

\(= 2800\)

\(\therefore\) 2800 coins were made.
PS7 Q5:
Diameter of the roller \(= 120\) cm, so \(r = 60\ \text{cm} = 0.6\) m; length \(h = 84\ \text{cm} = 0.84\) m.

In one rotation the roller levels its own curved surface.

Curved surface area \(= 2\pi r h = 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 0.6 \times 0.84\)

\(= 2 \times 22 \times 0.6 \times 0.12 = 3.168\ \text{m}^2\)

Area levelled in 200 rotations \(= 200 \times 3.168 = 633.6\ \text{m}^2\)

Expenditure \(= 633.6 \times 10 = \) Rs. 6336

\(\therefore\) the expenditure to level the ground is Rs. 6336.
PS7 Q6:
[Textbook note: the book prints the pair "452.16 sq.cm ; 3385.94 gm". Those two figures cannot come from one value of \(\pi\): 452.16 requires \(\pi = 3.14\), while 3385.94 requires \(\pi = \frac{22}{7}\). Worked consistently with \(\pi = 3.14\) the answers are 452.16 sq.cm and 3383.16 gm; worked consistently with \(\pi = \frac{22}{7}\) they are 452.57 sq.cm and 3386.24 gm.]

Diameter \(= 12\) cm, so the outer radius is \(R = 6\) cm.

Thickness \(= 0.01\ \text{m} = 1\) cm, so the inner radius is \(r = 6 - 1 = 5\) cm.

Taking \(\pi = 3.14\):

Outer surface area \(= 4\pi R^2 = 4 \times 3.14 \times 36\)

\(= 452.16\ \text{sq.cm}\)

Volume of the metal \(= \dfrac{4}{3}\pi\left(R^3 - r^3\right) = \dfrac{4}{3} \times 3.14 \times (216 - 125)\)

\(= \dfrac{4}{3} \times 3.14 \times 91 = 380.99\ \text{cm}^3\)

Mass \(=\) volume \(\times\) density \(= 380.99 \times 8.88\)

\(= 3383.16\) gm (approx.)

\(\therefore\) the outer surface area is 452.16 sq.cm and the mass is about 3383 gm.
PS7 Q7:
The bucket is a cylinder of diameter 28 cm, so \(r = 14\) cm, and height 20 cm.

Volume of the sand \(= \pi r^2 h = \pi \times 196 \times 20 = 3920\pi\ \text{cm}^3\)

The sand is then a cone of height 14 cm; let its base radius be \(R\).

\(\dfrac{1}{3}\pi R^2 \times 14 = 3920\pi\)

\(\therefore R^2 = \dfrac{3920 \times 3}{14} = 840\)

Base area of the cone \(= \pi R^2 = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 840\)

\(= 2640\ \text{sq.cm}\)

\(\therefore\) the base area of the cone is 2640 sq.cm.
PS7 Q8:
Volume of the sphere \(= \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi \times 9^3 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi \times 729 = 972\pi\ \text{cm}^3\)

The wire is a cylinder of diameter \(4\ \text{mm} = 0.4\) cm, so its radius is \(0.2\) cm.

Let the length of the wire be \(L\).

\(\pi (0.2)^2 L = 972\pi\)

\(0.04\,L = 972\)

\(\therefore L = \dfrac{972}{0.04} = 24300\ \text{cm} = 243\) m

\(\therefore\) the length of the wire is 243 metre.
PS7 Q9:
\(r = 6\) cm and the area of the sector is \(15\pi\) sq.cm.

Area of the sector \(= \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2\)

\(15\pi = \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi \times 36\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{\theta}{360} = \dfrac{15}{36} = \dfrac{5}{12}\)

\(\therefore \theta = \dfrac{5}{12} \times 360 = 150^\circ\)

Length of the arc \(= \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r = \dfrac{5}{12} \times 2\pi \times 6\)

\(= \dfrac{5}{12} \times 12\pi = 5\pi\) cm

\(\therefore\) the measure of the arc is \(150^\circ\) and its length is \(5\pi\) cm.
PS7 Q10:
PA \(= 8\) cm is a radius, and the distance of chord AB from the centre is 4 cm. Let M be the foot of the perpendicular from P to AB.

In right-angled \(\triangle\) PMA, AM \(= \sqrt{\text{PA}^2 - \text{PM}^2} = \sqrt{64 - 16} = \sqrt{48} = 4\sqrt{3}\) cm

\(\therefore\) AB \(= 2 \times 4\sqrt{3} = 8\sqrt{3} = 8 \times 1.73 = 13.84\) cm

Also PM \(= \dfrac{1}{2}\)PA, so \(\angle\) PAM \(= 30^\circ\) and \(\angle\) APM \(= 60^\circ\).

By symmetry \(\angle\) APB \(= 2 \times 60^\circ = 120^\circ\).

A(sector P-AXB) \(= \dfrac{120}{360} \times 3.14 \times 64 = \dfrac{200.96}{3} = 66.99\ \text{sq.cm}\)

A(\(\triangle\) APB) \(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{AB} \times \text{PM} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 13.84 \times 4 = 27.68\ \text{sq.cm}\)

Area of the shaded portion (the minor segment) \(= 66.99 - 27.68\)

\(= 39.31\ \text{sq.cm}\)

\(\therefore\) the area of the shaded portion is about 39.31 sq.cm.

(The book prints 39.28 sq.cm. The difference is only rounding: with the stated \(\sqrt{3} = 1.73\) the answer is 39.31, while a more precise \(\sqrt{3} = 1.732\) gives 39.27.)

PS7 Q12:
The completed activity is as follows.

Let the radius of the bigger circle be R and that of the smaller circle be r.

OA = OB = OC = OD = R and PQ = PA = r.

OQ = OB \(-\) BQ \(= \boxed{\text{R} - 9}\)

OE = OD \(-\) DE \(= \boxed{\text{R} - 5}\)

The chords QA and EF of the circle with centre P intersect inside it, so

OQ \(\times\) OA = OE \(\times\) OF

\(\boxed{(\text{R} - 9)} \times \text{R} = \boxed{(\text{R} - 5)} \times \boxed{(\text{R} - 5)}\) .......... \((\because\) OE = OF)

\(\text{R}^2 - 9\text{R} = \text{R}^2 - 10\text{R} + 25\)

\(-9\text{R} + 10\text{R} = 25\)

R \(= \boxed{25}\)

AB \(= 2\text{R} = 50\), so

AQ = 2r = AB \(-\) BQ

2r = 50 \(-\) 9 = 41

r \(= \boxed{\dfrac{41}{2}} = \boxed{20.5}\)

\(\therefore\) the radius of the bigger circle is 25 and that of the smaller circle is 20.5.
